flashcards.q: State the three Mom Test rules.
flashcards.a: Talk about their life, not your idea; ask about specifics in the past, not the future or hypotheticals; listen for commitments and behavior rather than compliments and opinions.

flashcards.q: What is the JTBD job-statement format?
flashcards.a: When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome]. E.g., 'When I'm on a 25-minute commute, I want something engaging and one-handed, so the drive feels short.' Customers hire products for progress; competing hires include non-obvious categories like sleep or Netflix.

flashcards.q: Name the four forces of progress and which side wins ties.
flashcards.a: Push of the current situation, pull of the new solution, anxiety about the new solution, habit/allegiance to the present way. Anxiety + habit win ties: users stay with painful-but-known tools unless push is evidenced by active workarounds and anxiety is reduced via trust/reversibility.

flashcards.q: Rank interview signal strength from strongest to weakest evidence.
flashcards.a: What they currently do > money/time already spent > specific past intentions > generic habit claims > predictions about their future behavior > opinions about your idea. Receipts (paid tools, built spreadsheets) beat praise; commitments of time/reputation beat both.

flashcards.q: Give the opportunity-score formula and interpret a high score.
flashcards.a: Opportunity = importance(1-10) x (10 - satisfaction(1-10)). High score means important AND poorly served (~80-90 range). Well-served jobs lose no matter how easy they are to demo; unimportant jobs lose regardless of dissatisfaction.

flashcards.q: What does an opportunity solution tree buy you when an experiment fails?
flashcards.a: You slide sideways to a sibling solution under the same validated opportunity instead of restarting from zero — the tree preserves validated problem framing and localizes failure. Prune an opportunity when it's well served/unimportant or when two distinct solutions both fail.

flashcards.q: List the kill ladder rungs with rough costs.
flashcards.a: Desk research/ticket mining (hours) -> 5-8 interviews (days) -> landing/smoke page with $100-300 cold ads (~1 week; <1-2% conversion kills demand story, 5%+ advances) -> concierge/Wizard-of-Oz (2-4 weeks) -> flagged prototype (weeks) -> full build (quarters). Each rung is ~5-20x cheaper than the next.

flashcards.q: Why can't 8 interviews size a market?
flashcards.a: Small-n qualitative work finds problems and mechanisms, never prevalence. NN/g's classic result (~5 users per round surface ~85% of usability issues) justifies small n for discovery rounds repeated fresh; sizing requires surveys or telemetry follow-up.

flashcards.q: What's the money question that separates real pain from stated pain?
flashcards.a: 'What's the most you've ever done to try to fix that?' Real pain leaves receipts: tools bought, spreadsheets built, hours spent. A claimed pain with zero attempted workarounds is a preference, not a problem.

flashcards.q: Where is AI legitimate in discovery and where does it lie?
flashcards.a: Legitimate: transcription, theme clustering across transcripts, mining reviews/tickets at corpus scale, drafting follow-ups. It lies when simulating respondents (synthetic personas have zero evidentiary weight), inventing coherence among weak signals, or smoothing away disconfirming quotes in summaries — read raw excerpts before decisions.

flashcards.q: How do you run discovery when the CEO demands competitor parity next quarter?
flashcards.a: Reframe as de-risking speed: compress to 1-2 weeks — mine competitor reviews for weaknesses, interview users who tried their version, define the win metric, propose smallest instrumented slice. Minimum fallback if there's truly no time: baseline captured pre-launch plus written kill/iterate thresholds.

flashcards.q: When do you stop discovering and start building?
flashcards.a: When (1) an opportunity clearly tops alternatives on importance x dissatisfaction per PRE-AGREED numeric rules, (2) at least one solution survived its cheapest behavioral test, and (3) remaining uncertainty is execution scale, not demand direction. Timebox guard: after two clean ladder rungs without triggering kill conditions, build the flag and let telemetry take over.
